claims.text: The multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy forms a relatively uniform protective oxide layer across its phases under ambient conditions.
Mechanical wear removes segments of the protective oxide film and exposes fresh alloy surfaces.
Compositional differences between phases create local galvanic cells at phase boundaries.
Different phases have different electrochemical stabilities.
At elevated temperature, freshly exposed areas undergo rapid localized corrosion at phase interfaces.
Localized corrosion at phase interfaces undermines the mechanical integrity of the phases.
Corrosion-induced weakening exacerbates subsequent wear damage.
The feedback between oxide disruption, localized corrosion, and mechanical weakening produces degradation greater than the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce significantly greater total degradation than the isolated conditions.
Under simultaneous exposure, corrosion pits will be deeper and more frequent at phase boundaries.
Under simultaneous exposure, wear will be more severe because of loss of the protective oxide.
A temperature around 400°C provides sufficient thermal energy to enhance corrosion kinetics in the proposed system.
The proposed mechanism requires wear loads that partially remove the oxide film without completely destroying it.
The mechanism may not apply to alloys lacking distinct phase boundaries.
Parallel simultaneous, wear-only, and corrosion-only tests at 400°C constitute the proposed controlled comparison.
Failure of combined degradation to exceed the additive isolated effects, or absence of localized damage at oxide breakages and phase boundaries, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
